question: Which pattern is most effective at preventing cascading failures when a downstream dependency becomes slow (not down)?
options: Increasing the retry count with longer timeouts
Setting aggressive timeouts combined with bulkhead isolation
Adding more instances of the calling service
Switching to synchronous communication
explanation: A slow dependency is more dangerous than a dead one — requests pile up, threads/connections exhaust, and the failure cascades upstream. Aggressive timeouts (fail fast) prevent thread exhaustion, and bulkhead isolation (separate thread pools per dependency) ensures one slow service can't consume all resources. More retries with longer timeouts makes it worse.

question: What triggers a circuit breaker to transition from 'closed' (healthy) to 'open' (tripped)?
options: A single failed request to the downstream service
The failure rate exceeding a configured threshold within a sliding window
The downstream service sending an explicit 'circuit-open' header
A deployment event detected by the service mesh
explanation: Circuit breakers track failure rates (errors, timeouts) over a sliding window (time-based or count-based). When failures exceed the threshold (e.g., 50% of last 20 requests), the breaker opens and short-circuits all calls for a configurable timeout, returning a fallback or error immediately instead of waiting for the failing service.

question: The 'bulkhead' resilience pattern is named after ship compartments. In software, it prevents:
options: Data corruption across microservices by isolating databases
A failure in one dependency from exhausting shared resources (threads, connections) and taking down unrelated functionality
Unauthorized access between service boundaries
Network partitions from affecting service availability
explanation: Bulkheads isolate resource pools per dependency or call path. If Service A calls Service B and Service C using the same thread pool, a slow Service B can exhaust all threads and block calls to the healthy Service C. Separate pools (bulkheads) ensure each dependency can only consume its allocated resources, containing blast radius.

question: A 'retry storm' occurs when multiple clients simultaneously retry failed requests. What is the standard mitigation?
options: Disable retries entirely
Exponential backoff with jitter
Increase the server's connection pool size
Switch from HTTP to gRPC
explanation: Exponential backoff spaces retries further apart with each attempt (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s...). Adding randomized jitter ensures clients don't all retry at the exact same intervals, spreading load. Without jitter, synchronized retries create periodic spikes. This is a standard pattern in AWS SDKs and gRPC libraries.

question: When would you choose gRPC over REST for service-to-service communication?
options: When you need browser clients to call the API directly without a proxy
When you need high-throughput, low-latency communication with strict schema contracts between internal services
When the API must be easily testable with curl
When you want maximum flexibility in response format negotiation
explanation: gRPC uses HTTP/2 (multiplexing, header compression), Protocol Buffers (compact binary serialization), and strong schema contracts (.proto files) — yielding 2-10x smaller payloads and lower latency than JSON/REST. Ideal for internal service-to-service calls. REST is better for public APIs, browser clients, and discoverability.

question: Cursor-based pagination is preferred over offset-based pagination because:
options: It uses less memory on the client side
It is immune to data drift — insertions/deletions between pages don't cause skipped or duplicated items
It allows jumping to arbitrary page numbers efficiently
It is simpler to implement in SQL
explanation: Offset pagination (OFFSET 100 LIMIT 10) breaks when rows are inserted/deleted between requests — items shift position, causing duplicates or gaps. Cursor pagination uses a stable pointer (e.g., 'after: last_seen_id') so each page starts from a fixed anchor regardless of mutations. Trade-off: you lose the ability to jump to 'page 50.'

question: An API endpoint is 'idempotent' if:
options: It always returns the same response regardless of input
Making the same request multiple times produces the same result as making it once
It can only be called once per session
It never modifies server state
explanation: Idempotency means repeated identical requests have the same effect as a single request. This is critical for reliability — if a client times out on a payment API call, it must safely retry without double-charging. Common implementation: the client sends an idempotency key; the server deduplicates by storing results keyed by that token.

question: GraphQL's primary advantage over REST for a mobile client consuming data from multiple backend services is:
options: It is always faster due to binary serialization
The client can request exactly the fields it needs in a single query, avoiding over-fetching and multiple round trips
It automatically handles caching better than REST
It requires no schema definition
explanation: REST APIs return fixed response shapes, so a mobile screen needing data from /users, /posts, and /comments makes 3 calls and receives many unused fields. GraphQL lets the client specify exactly which fields from which types it needs in one request, reducing bandwidth (critical on mobile) and latency (one round trip vs. many).

question: Which HTTP method is NOT idempotent by specification?
options: GET
PUT
DELETE
POST
explanation: Per HTTP spec: GET, PUT, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS are idempotent — repeating them has the same effect. POST is not idempotent by default: POSTing the same order twice creates two orders. PATCH is also not guaranteed idempotent (depends on the operation). This is why payment APIs use idempotency keys on POST requests.

question: A dead letter queue (DLQ) is used to:
options: Store messages that have been successfully processed for audit purposes
Capture messages that repeatedly fail processing so they don't block the main queue
Prioritize high-importance messages over low-importance ones
Encrypt messages at rest in the primary queue
explanation: When a message fails processing after a configured number of retries (e.g., 3 attempts), it's moved to the DLQ instead of being retried forever or dropped. This prevents poison messages from blocking the queue while preserving them for investigation. DLQs should be monitored — a growing DLQ signals a systemic problem.

question: Back pressure in a message processing system means:
options: The system drops all incoming messages when overloaded
Consumers signal producers to slow down when they cannot keep up, preventing resource exhaustion
Messages are processed in reverse order during high load
The queue automatically scales to infinite capacity
explanation: Back pressure is a flow-control mechanism where downstream systems communicate their capacity limits upstream. Without it, a fast producer overwhelms a slow consumer — the queue grows unboundedly, memory exhausts, and the system crashes. Implementations include blocking producers, returning HTTP 429, or using bounded queues that reject when full.

question: When choosing between a message queue (SQS/RabbitMQ) and a log-based broker (Kafka), a key deciding factor is:
options: Kafka is always faster for all workloads
Traditional queues delete messages after consumption; log-based brokers retain messages and support multiple independent consumers replaying from any offset
Message queues support higher throughput than Kafka
Log-based brokers don't support consumer groups
explanation: Message queues use destructive reads — once consumed, a message is gone (or invisible). Kafka retains messages for a configurable period, allowing multiple consumer groups to read the same stream independently and replay from any offset. Choose queues for simple task distribution; choose Kafka when you need event sourcing, replay, or fan-out to independent consumers.

question: To guarantee exactly-once processing semantics with at-least-once delivery, consumers must:
options: Use a FIFO queue, which handles this automatically
Implement idempotent message handling — track processed message IDs and skip duplicates
Set the visibility timeout to infinity
Disable message retries entirely
explanation: Most queue systems provide at-least-once delivery (messages may be delivered more than once due to retries, network issues). To achieve effectively-exactly-once processing, consumers must be idempotent: track processed message IDs (in a database or cache) and skip duplicates. FIFO queues reduce but don't eliminate duplicates across failure scenarios.

question: What happens when a message queue consumer crashes AFTER processing a message but BEFORE acknowledging it?
options: The message is permanently lost
The message becomes visible again after the visibility timeout expires and is redelivered to another consumer
The queue automatically detects the crash and marks the message as processed
The message is moved directly to the dead letter queue
explanation: Most queues (SQS, RabbitMQ) use a visibility timeout / acknowledgment model: a consumed message becomes invisible to other consumers for a timeout period. If not acknowledged (acked) before timeout — whether due to crash or slow processing — the message reappears and is redelivered. This is why consumers must be idempotent.
